solution:
Each row must carry a quantity, its SI unit and the property that belongs to it.

| I | II | III |
|---|---|---|
| Mass | kg | Measure of inertia |
| Weight | N | Depends on height |
| Acceleration due to gravity | m/s² | Zero at the centre |
| Gravitational constant | Nm²/kg² | Same in the entire universe |

The chapter supplies every pairing. **Mass** — “the SI unit of mass is kg” and “according to Newton’s first law, it is the measure of the inertia of an object”. **Weight** — “weight being a force, its SI unit is Newton”, and since \(W = mg\) while g falls as we rise above the surface, the weight depends on height. **Acceleration due to gravity** — “the unit of g in SI units is m/s²”, and going deeper into the earth reduces both r and the mass M that pulls on the object, so g keeps decreasing and reaches zero at the centre. **Gravitational constant** — its unit is Nm²/kg², and it is called the *universal* gravitational constant precisely because its value is the same everywhere in the universe.

**Mass** is the amount of matter present in an object. It is a scalar, its SI unit is the kilogram, it measures the inertia of the object, and its value is the same everywhere — the chapter says it “does not change even when we go to another planet”.

**Weight** is the force with which the earth attracts the object, \(W = mg\). It is a vector directed towards the centre of the earth and its SI unit is the newton.

On Mars the **mass would be the same** and the **weight would be different**. The mass is a property of the object itself, so carrying it to Mars changes nothing. The weight is \(mg\), and the chapter states that \(g = GM/R^2\) depends only on the mass and radius of the planet — “every planet and satellite has different mass and radius. Hence … the values of g on their surfaces are different.” Mars has a different mass and radius from the earth, so g there differs and the weight differs with it.

**(i) Free fall.** “Whenever an object moves under the influence of the force of gravity alone, it is said to be falling freely.” In free fall the initial velocity is zero and the velocity goes on increasing because of the acceleration due to gravity. True free fall is possible only in vacuum, because in air a frictional force and a buoyant force also act on the object.

**(ii) Acceleration due to gravity.** The gravitational force of the earth on a body produces an acceleration in it; that acceleration is called the acceleration due to gravity and is written g. It is directed towards the centre of the earth, i.e. vertically downwards, its SI unit is m/s², and on the surface of the earth \(g = GM/R^2 = 9.77\ \text{m/s}^2\). It does not depend on any property of the falling object.

**(iii) Escape velocity.** As the initial velocity given to a ball thrown upward is increased, it reaches greater and greater heights; above a particular value of that initial velocity the ball overcomes the downward pull of the earth altogether and never falls back. That value is the escape velocity, \(v_{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R} = \sqrt{2gR}\), which for the earth is 11.2 km/s.

**(iv) Centripetal force.** “A force acts on any object moving along a circle and it is directed towards the centre of the circle. This is called the centripetal force.” ‘Centripetal’ means centre-seeking. For an object of mass m moving with speed v in a circle of radius r its magnitude is \(F = mv^2/r\).

**Kepler’s three laws.**

1. The orbit of a planet is an ellipse with the Sun at one of the foci.
2. The line joining the planet and the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal intervals of time.
3. The square of the period of revolution of a planet around the Sun is directly proportional to the cube of its mean distance from the Sun: \(T^2 \propto r^3\), i.e. \(T^2/r^3 = K\), a constant.

**How they led Newton to the inverse square law.** It is the third law that does the work. Take a planet of mass m moving in a circular orbit of radius r with speed v. Its circular motion needs a centripetal force

\(F = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}\)

In one revolution the planet covers the perimeter \(2\pi r\) in time T, so \(v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}\) and

\(F = \dfrac{m}{r}\left(\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}mr}{T^{2}}\)

Multiplying and dividing by \(r^2\),

\(F = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}m}{r^{2}}\cdot\dfrac{r^{3}}{T^{2}}\)

Kepler’s third law now says the last factor \(r^3/T^2\) is the constant K, so

\(F = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}m}{K}\cdot\dfrac{1}{r^{2}} \quad\text{i.e.}\quad F \propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}\)

So the force holding a planet in its orbit must fall off as the inverse square of its distance from the Sun. Newton identified this force with the force of gravity and therefore postulated the inverse square law of gravitation. Kepler himself, the chapter notes, “had no explanation as to why planets obey these laws” — he obtained them purely from observation, and Newton supplied the reason.

Let the stone be thrown up with initial velocity u and let it rise to a height h.

**Going up.** The acceleration is \(-g\), opposite to the velocity, and at the highest point the velocity is zero. By Newton’s first equation of motion, \(v = u + at\):

\(0 = u - g\,t_{up} \quad\Rightarrow\quad t_{up} = \dfrac{u}{g}\)

The height reached follows from \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\): \(0 = u^2 - 2gh\), so \(h = \dfrac{u^{2}}{2g}\).

**Coming down.** The stone now starts from rest at that height, so it is in free fall with \(u = 0\) and \(a = +g\). By \(s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^{2}\):

\(h = \dfrac{1}{2}g\,t_{down}^{2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad t_{down} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}\)

Putting \(h = u^{2}/2g\) into this,

\(t_{down} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{g}\cdot\dfrac{u^{2}}{2g}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{u^{2}}{g^{2}}} = \dfrac{u}{g}\)

So \(t_{down} = t_{up} = u/g\): the time taken to go up equals the time taken to come down. The chapter’s own worked example shows the same thing numerically — a ball reaching 4.05 m takes 0.9 s to come down, “it will take the same time to go up”, and the total time is 1.8 s.

The difficulty of dragging an object along the floor comes from friction, and friction depends on how hard the object presses on the floor — that is, on its **weight**, not on its mass.

The chapter gives the weight as \(W = mg\). The mass m is a property of the object and does not change. So if g suddenly became twice as large, the weight of the object would also become twice as large:

\(W' = m(2g) = 2mg = 2W\)

The object would press on the floor twice as hard, the frictional force opposing the sliding would double with it, and we would have to pull twice as hard to move it — it becomes two times more difficult. (Note that the *mass* being dragged is unchanged; it is only the pressing force, and hence the friction, that has doubled.)

Use \(g = \dfrac{GM}{r^{2}}\), where r is the distance from the centre of the earth and M is the part of the earth’s mass that pulls the object.

As the chapter explains under ‘change with depth’, going inside the earth reduces r, which by itself would raise g — but “the part of the earth which contributes towards the gravitational force felt by the object also decreases. Which means that the value of M to be used … also decreases. As a combined result of change in r and M, the value of g decreases as we go deep inside the earth.”

At the very centre this reasoning reaches its limit. There is no part of the earth left *below* the object to pull it inward; the earth’s matter now surrounds it completely and on all sides. The pull of every piece of the earth is balanced by the pull of the matter diametrically opposite it, so the net gravitational force on a body at the centre is zero. Since \(g\) is the acceleration that this force produces, **g is zero at the centre of the earth** — which is why the exercise table lists ‘zero at the centre’ as a property of g.

By Kepler’s third law the square of the period of revolution is directly proportional to the cube of the distance:

\(\dfrac{T^{2}}{R^{3}} = K \quad (\text{a constant})\)

At distance R the period is T, so \(T^{2} = K R^{3}\).

Let the period at distance 2R be \(T_1\). Applying the same law,

\(T_1^{2} = K(2R)^{3} = 8KR^{3}\)

Dividing the second result by the first,

\(\dfrac{T_1^{2}}{T^{2}} = \dfrac{8KR^{3}}{KR^{3}} = 8\)

\(\therefore\ T_1^{2} = 8T^{2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_1 = \sqrt{8}\,T\)

So a planet twice as far from the star takes \(\sqrt{8}\,T\) (about 2.83 T) to complete one revolution. Note that the constant K cancels, so the result holds whatever the star.

The object is in free fall, so its initial velocity is zero.

**Given:** \(s = 5\ \text{m}\), \(t = 5\ \text{s}\), \(u = 0\), \(a = g\).

Using Newton’s second equation of motion, \(s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^{2}\):

\(5 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}\,g\,(5)^{2} = \dfrac{25g}{2}\)

\(g = \dfrac{2 \times 5}{25} = \dfrac{10}{25} = 0.4\ \text{m/s}^{2}\)

**The value of g on that planet is 0.4 m/s²**, which agrees with the answer printed in the textbook. It is far smaller than the earth’s 9.8 m/s², as it must be for an object to need five whole seconds to fall only 5 m.

The acceleration due to gravity on the surface of a planet is \(g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}\), which the chapter notes “depends only on the mass M and radius R” of the planet.

**Given:** \(R_A = \tfrac{1}{2}R_B\), i.e. \(R_B = 2R_A\); mass of A is \(M_A\); and \(g_B = \tfrac{1}{2}g_A\). Let the mass of B be \(M_B\).

\(g_A = \dfrac{GM_A}{R_A^{2}}\ ,\qquad g_B = \dfrac{GM_B}{R_B^{2}} = \dfrac{GM_B}{(2R_A)^{2}} = \dfrac{GM_B}{4R_A^{2}}\)

The condition \(g_B = \tfrac{1}{2}g_A\) gives

\(\dfrac{GM_B}{4R_A^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{GM_A}{R_A^{2}}\)

G and \(R_A^{2}\) cancel from both sides:

\(\dfrac{M_B}{4} = \dfrac{M_A}{2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad M_B = 2M_A\)

**The mass of B must be \(2M_A\)**, which is the answer printed in the textbook. The result is worth reading: B is twice as heavy as A yet its g is only half, because doubling the radius divides g by four and that outweighs the doubling of the mass.

**Mass.** Mass is the amount of matter in the object and, as the chapter states, “its value does not change even when we go to another planet”. So the mass on the moon is still **5 kg**.

**Weight.** Weight is \(W = mg\), so it changes in exactly the same proportion as g. Given \(g_{moon} = \tfrac{1}{6}g_{earth}\),

\(W_{moon} = m\,g_{moon} = m\cdot\dfrac{g_{earth}}{6} = \dfrac{W_{earth}}{6} = \dfrac{49}{6} = 8.17\ \text{N}\)

**On the moon the mass is 5 kg and the weight is 8.17 N**, matching the answer printed in the textbook. (The given data are consistent: \(49 \div 5 = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2\), the value of g on the earth.)

**Going up.** The object rises until its velocity is zero, with acceleration \(-g\).

**Given:** \(s = 500\ \text{m}\), \(v = 0\), \(a = -g = -10\ \text{m/s}^{2}\).

By Newton’s third equation of motion, \(v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as\):

\(0 = u^{2} + 2(-10)(500) = u^{2} - 10000\)

\(u^{2} = 10000 \quad\Rightarrow\quad u = 100\ \text{m/s}\)

**Time.** By \(v = u + at\), the time to reach the top is

\(0 = 100 - 10\,t_{up} \quad\Rightarrow\quad t_{up} = 10\ \text{s}\)

The time to come down equals the time to go up, so the total time is

\(t = 2 \times 10 = 20\ \text{s}\)

**The initial velocity was 100 m/s and the object takes 20 s to come back**, which agrees with the answer printed in the textbook.

The ball falls off the table, so it starts from rest and is in free fall.

**Given:** \(u = 0\), \(t = 1\ \text{s}\), \(a = g = 10\ \text{m/s}^{2}\).

**Speed on reaching the ground**, from \(v = u + at\):

\(v = 0 + 10 \times 1 = 10\ \text{m/s}\)

**Height of the table**, from \(s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^{2}\):

\(s = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (1)^{2} = 5\ \text{m}\)

**The ball reaches the ground at 10 m/s and the table is 5 m high**, matching the answer printed in the textbook.

**Given:** \(m_1 = 6 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}\), \(m_2 = 7.4 \times 10^{22}\ \text{kg}\), \(G = 6.7 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{kg}^{-2}\), and \(d = 3.84 \times 10^{5}\ \text{km}\).

**Convert the distance to metres first** — this is where the calculation is usually lost. \(1\ \text{km} = 10^{3}\ \text{m}\), so \(d = 3.84 \times 10^{5} \times 10^{3} = 3.84 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m}\).

By Newton’s law of gravitation,

\(F = \dfrac{G\,m_1 m_2}{d^{2}} = \dfrac{6.7 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 7.4 \times 10^{22}}{(3.84 \times 10^{8})^{2}}\)

Numerator: \(6.7 \times 6 \times 7.4 = 297.5\), and \(10^{-11} \times 10^{24} \times 10^{22} = 10^{35}\), giving \(2.975 \times 10^{37}\).

Denominator: \((3.84)^{2} = 14.75\) and \((10^{8})^{2} = 10^{16}\), giving \(1.475 \times 10^{17}\).

\(F = \dfrac{2.975 \times 10^{37}}{1.475 \times 10^{17}} = 2.02 \times 10^{20}\ \text{N}\)

**The gravitational force between the earth and the moon is about \(2 \times 10^{20}\) N**, which is the answer printed in the textbook.

**Given:** mass of the earth \(m = 6 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}\), \(d = 1.5 \times 10^{11}\ \text{m}\), \(F = 3.5 \times 10^{22}\ \text{N}\), \(G = 6.7 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{kg}^{-2}\). Let the mass of the Sun be M.

Newton’s law of gravitation gives \(F = \dfrac{GMm}{d^{2}}\), so rearranging for M,

\(M = \dfrac{F\,d^{2}}{G\,m}\)

\(M = \dfrac{3.5 \times 10^{22} \times (1.5 \times 10^{11})^{2}}{6.7 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24}}\)

Numerator: \((1.5 \times 10^{11})^{2} = 2.25 \times 10^{22}\), so the numerator is \(3.5 \times 2.25 = 7.875\), i.e. \(7.875 \times 10^{44}\).

Denominator: \(6.7 \times 6 = 40.2\) and \(10^{-11} \times 10^{24} = 10^{13}\), i.e. \(4.02 \times 10^{14}\).

\(M = \dfrac{7.875 \times 10^{44}}{4.02 \times 10^{14}} = 1.96 \times 10^{30}\ \text{kg}\)

**The mass of the Sun is about \(1.96 \times 10^{30}\) kg**, which is the answer printed in the textbook — roughly 3,30,000 times the mass of the earth.
